Using a categorical recurrent state-space model, CommDreamer compresses multimodal measurement histories into a coordinate-invariant latent belief, enabling the UAV to foresee deep shadow zones and train a lightweight online policy purely via multi-step latent imagination without prior maps or antenna patterns. Zero-shot evaluations across unseen urban morphologies in our open-source ray-tracing simulator, AeroCity-RT, show that CommDreamer converges within 150 episodes where model-free reinforcement learning fails to complete flights, achieving 100.0% mission success with zero collisions while lifting median route SINR to 8.02 dB and cutting effective SINR outage by over 50% relative to radio-blind world-model and reactive LiDAR baselines.

entries.title: Laguerre-MPPI
entries.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral control (MPPI) is a sampling-based control method that handles nonlinear dynamics and non-convex costs without gradient information. Since MPPI samples the entire input sequence, longer prediction horizons lead to a higher-dimensional sampling space, potentially degrading control performance. This paper proposes Laguerre-MPPI, which parameterizes the control input sequence using discrete-time Laguerre basis functions and samples the basis coefficients. The resulting search dimension is independent of the prediction horizon. Hence, a longer prediction horizon does not require more samples to maintain the sampling density. For linear systems with quadratic costs, we derive a closed-loop stability condition in the infinite-sample limit. Under finite sampling, we provide a closed-form expression for the limit of the ratio of the effective sample size to the number of samples. We also show that the upper bound of this limit for Laguerre-MPPI is no lower than that for conventional MPPI. Numerical experiments demonstrate smoother inputs in obstacle avoidance and maintained performance over long horizons. Moreover, they verify the lower bound on the number of samples given by the finite-sample analysis.

entries.title: Adaptive Guidance for 3GPP Ambient IoT Contention-Based Random Access
entries.abstract: The emerging ambient Internet of Things (A-IoT) envisions connectivity among large populations of low-cost, energy-constrained devices. Supporting such connectivity requires efficient coordination of device access, particularly in reader-triggered operation, where multiple devices may respond to paging over limited shared radio resources. Indeed, simultaneous responses can lead to severe contention, delayed transmissions, and lost reports. This article explores how compact extensions to the current 3GPP Release-19 signaling framework could enable more selective and adaptive device access. The proposed approach allows readers to broadcast compact access guidance, which devices interpret according to their local conditions, while optional feedback supports continuous adaptation. Through a device-reporting case study, we demonstrate how such coordination can improve report delivery and timeliness under congested conditions, while highlighting the trade-offs across different network configurations. We also examine practical signaling considerations and discuss opportunities for more intelligent, adaptive, and resilient protocols.

entries.title: Scalable Vehicle Charging Coordination for Online Operations: A Column Generation Approach
entries.abstract: We consider an electric vehicle charging scheduling problem for long-haul freight transport. To mitigate unforeseen waiting times caused by congestion and limited charger capacity, we consider a coordinated scheduling approach that prioritizes scalable, computationally efficient scheduling for ongoing or online operations. We formulate the problem as a set partitioning model and develop a column generation framework with a label-correcting algorithm to solve it efficiently. We assess the scalability of our algorithm through both theoretical complexity analysis and empirical measurements, highlighting the role of feasibility and dominance pruning in limiting label growth. Finally, using freight telematics data from Sweden, we show that the proposed method computes optimized schedules for realistic instances with 1000 vehicles within seconds and reduces vehicle operation downtime by 78.6% compared to uncoordinated scheduling.

entries.title: Dynamic and Risk-Aware Procurement of Fast Frequency Response from Electric Vehicles and Heat Pumps
entries.abstract: Low-inertia power systems increasingly rely on Fast Frequency Response (FFR) to keep the frequency nadir above under-frequency load-shedding thresholds without oversized Frequency Containment Reserve or synchronous inertia. This paper proposes two complementary methodologies that interface with an existing day-ahead FFR capacity market. On the Transmission System Operator (TSO) side, a dynamic procurement rule maps forecasted kinetic energy and contingency magnitude onto an offline neighborhood-need surface, yielding interval-wise FFR capacity requests rather than constant seasonal or annual volumes. On the aggregator side, a risk-aware, TSO-certifiable bidding strategy quantifies reliable FFR capacity from fleets of electric vehicles (EVs) and heat pumps (HPs) by offering lower conditional quantiles of day-ahead headroom at a prescribed delivery reliability. The resulting requests and offers are cleared through a pay-as-bid capacity auction. A Cyprus 2025 case study shows that dynamic neighborhood-based procurement yields an annual clearing cost of about EUR 476,000, which is 30%-33% lower than the seasonal and annual static rules and also below the UFLS VoLL of EUR 637,500 estimated from the fifteen real 2025 events with fmin <= 49 Hz. EV and HP offers meet their target delivery reliabilities, and RMS validation finds 46 of 50 operating points above 49 Hz at both full and 85% FFR delivery.

entries.title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
entries.abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel “box” quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i) mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii) each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max–min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy–violation trade-off.

entries.title: Physical Layer Security for Digital Semantic Communication: A Bit-Level Perspective
entries.abstract: Digital semantic communication requires reliable recovery of task-relevant information at a legitimate receiver while limiting source reconstruction by an eavesdropper. Uniform bit protection, however, does not account for the heterogeneous reliability and secrecy requirements of semantic bits. This paper proposes a bit-level physical layer security (PLS) framework that learns these requirements and incorporates them into physical-layer resource allocation. We first introduce a wiretap semantic feature channel whose two-stage training learns per-bit target bit-flip probabilities for the legitimate receiver (Bob) and the eavesdropper (Eve). These targets characterize the reliability requirements at Bob and the secrecy protection requirements against Eve. Based on the learned targets, we formulate a joint power and artificial-noise (AN) allocation problem for a multiple-input single-output wiretap channel under a worst-case angular-separation model. For a given target profile, the optimal information-AN power split admits a closed-form solution, and the per-bit power allocation is obtained by water-filling. We further develop a leakage-aware selection method among multiple learned-target profiles and extend the design to multiple-input multiple-output channels. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a better trade-off between preserving reconstruction quality at Bob and degrading that at Eve than uniform power allocation and the evaluated learning-based secure semantic communication schemes.

entries.title: Control-Aware Separating Hyperplanes for Control Barrier Functions in Planar Navigation
entries.abstract: Separating hyperplanes are widely used in Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based collision avoidance, yet their orientations strongly govern control intervention-the deviation of the applied control from the robot's nominal command. Existing methods typically select hyperplane orientations from geometry alone. Jointly optimizing orientations and control yields a continuous, non-convex problem in which local nonlinear solvers suffer from initialization sensitivity, local minima, and unpredictable latency, while discretized orientation grids scale exponentially with obstacle count. For planar navigation of a polygonal robot among polygonal obstacles, we present a solver-free, control-aware separating hyperplane selection method that directly computes a global optimum of this joint problem at each step whenever it is feasible. Exploiting the geometry of Minkowski difference polygons, we reduce this continuous non-convex optimization to evaluating a polynomial-size set of candidate control interventions via closed-form algebraic checks, selecting the feasible candidate of minimum norm. Across 250 simulated navigation scenarios, our method reduces cumulative intervention cost by 3.6% at the median and 27.3% at the 90th percentile compared to a local nonlinear solver, and completion time by 0.6% and 5.6%, respectively. In scalability benchmarks, it achieves a 6.1x per-step speedup at 16 simultaneous obstacles.

entries.title: Estimation-Aware Reachability
entries.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability computes the states from which a system can be kept safe under worst-case disturbances, but it assumes the state is known exactly, whereas real robots act on noisy estimates whose uncertainty evolves with their motion. We extend Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability to the robot's belief, estimate and uncertainty, treating unexpected measurements as a bounded adversary and enlarging the unsafe set by the current uncertainty, so that certified states are safe with a prescribed probability. The formulation is compatible with existing solvers. In simulation, the resulting safety filters nearly eliminate the collisions of certaintyequivalent HJ and are less conservative than equally safe uncertainty-padding baselines. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/HimanshuPaudel/Estimation-Aware-Reachability

entries.title: Approximating Anisotropic Solar Radiation Pressure
entries.abstract: Solar radiation pressure (SRP) significantly influences satellite dynamics in high-altitude orbits, depending not only on the satellite's trajectory and attitude but also on its surface optical characteristics. Metallic surfaces, such as solar cells with periodic metal bars, exhibit anisotropic reflection that produces an anisotropic SRP. The difficulty in dealing with anisotropic SRP arises because anisotropic SRP does not have a general analytical solution, and accurate computation therefore requires numerical integration. An analytical formulation of anisotropic SRP is useful for stability analysis and controller design for satellites that exploit SRP. To this end, this paper derives an analytical approximation method to calculate the anisotropic SRP modeled with the Ashikhmin-Shirley model. The anisotropy is approximated using multiple spherical Gaussians. Because the product of spherical Gaussians is also a spherical Gaussian, anisotropic reflection can be expressed in an analytically tractable form. The approximation accuracy of the anisotropic SRP is numerically verified for two cases: weak anisotropy and strong anisotropy.
entries.comment: 33 pages, 21 figures, 4 tables. Accepted manuscript of the article published in Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics

entries.title: Mitigating the Grid Impact of Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers via High-Fidelity Model Flexibility
entries.abstract: Gigawatt-scale artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are being connected at a single point of interconnection (POI) faster than transmission can be reinforced, yet studies of their flexibility rely on DC power flow and simplified load envelopes that omit voltage, cooling dynamics, and workload deadlines. This paper addresses this gap by embedding a high-fidelity AIDC model, with separate inference and training pools, hall thermal mass, PV, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with reactive capability, and a STATCOM, in a five-minute multi-period AC optimal power flow. Simulations on the RTS-GMLC test system show that active-power flexibility mitigates local price spikes and relieves congestion, whereas reactive support from the BESS inverter or a STATCOM is needed to keep the POI voltage away from sagging around its 0.95 pu limit. Sensitivity analyses show that cost-driven charging of large batteries can induce new morning congestion and that storage largely substitutes for wider workload deferral.

entries.title: Measuring the Conservatism of Latent Safety Filters for World Models
entries.abstract: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.

entries.title: Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation
entries.abstract: Multi-tenant data center (DC) facilities rent computing capacity on demand, placing controllable load within reach of anyone willing to pay for it. This paper considers a stealthy adversary who rents workstations and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model (LLM) training, synchronizing their consumption into large periodic oscillations while each workload remains individually indistinguishable from benign training. The periodicity of such workloads is characterized experimentally and used to model facility consumption, showing that oscillations emerge from the interaction of concurrent workloads, whether aligned by an adversary or arising naturally. A combined small- and large-signal assessment, under a hardware-grounded threat model whose feasibility is supported by experiments on a supercomputer, locates the oscillatory weak points of the network. MW-scale oscillations are shown to saturate the generators' control limiters, amplifying their effect, while Floquet analysis reveals a lightly damped mode emerging near the forcing frequency. To counter both origins, signal-energy-based detection and mitigation are proposed, the latter re-timing the workloads to minimize the facility's oscillatory energy. The approach is validated through power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network.

entries.title: Radar-Native Control Barrier Functions: Doppler Range Rate as a Measured Barrier Derivative
entries.abstract: Safe control around dynamic obstacles requires information about both distance and relative motion. Range-based filters commonly reconstruct the required range rate from successive range measurements or from obstacle-state estimators, which can introduce estimator delay or sensitivity to range noise when obstacle motion changes. A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar measures radial relative velocity directly through Doppler. We use this measurement as the derivative of an ego-centered range control barrier function (CBF) and obtain a closed-form filter on the robot's forward velocity. A measurement margin constructed from sensor error bounds accounts for errors in range, Doppler, ego velocity, and bearing. In 508 paired encounters within the platform's retreat capability, direct Doppler produces two buffer incursions, compared with 15 for a constant-acceleration and 25 for a constant-velocity Kalman filter. On a Unitree Go1, the controller stops at 0.777 ±0.015 m against the predicted 0.758 m and reacts to a farther approaching object while a nearer static return remains. The guarantee covers the longitudinal range channel under bounded measurement errors and continuously available detections. Direct Doppler removes the need to reconstruct range rate in the safety loop, reducing the delay between a change in obstacle motion and its effect on the safety command.

entries.title: A Dynamic Model and Stability Analysis of a Grid-Interactive Data Center
entries.abstract: The rapid growth of data centers is creating new interactions between computational workload and power-system dynamics, with potentially significant implications for grid stability. We develop a four-dimensional nonlinear dynamical model of a data center campus interconnected with the bulk power system through a modified Single Machine Infinite Bus system. The model couples generator swing dynamics with a fluid-limit model of computational workload backlog and a grid-interactive data center power controller that incorporates both frequency feedback and computational backpressure. This formulation captures the coupled evolution of generator frequency, rotor angle, computational workload, and data center power consumption, providing a framework for studying the stability implications of flexible data center operation.

entries.title: Modeling and Stability of Power Systems With Coupled Data Center and Grid Dynamics
entries.abstract: The growing deployment of data centers poses challenges for power-system operation. However, data centers possess flexible resources that can be leveraged to mitigate their impact on the grid and provide grid services. This paper develops a linear-affine dynamic model of a transmission network with multiple data centers, explicitly coupling electromechanical grid dynamics with data center power demand and computational backlog. Grid-aware computing policies are incorporated to represent how data centers adjust their computational power in response to grid frequency deviations and workload backlog. The proposed framework provides a tractable means of investigating the interactions between multiple data centers and the transmission grid and assessing the potential of flexible computing to support power-system stability.

entries.title: Averting `Gravity': Launch Control and the Limits of Collision Avoidance in Low Earth Orbit Operations
entries.abstract: As large constellations fill low Earth orbit, the risk of a runaway collision cascade has become a central concern of space operations. Debris population models treat collision avoidance as a fixed input, although the capacity to screen potential collisions and plan maneuvers degrades as debris accumulates. Using a stylized multi-layer queueing network model, we show that collision avoidance capabilities that saturate as the in-custody fragment count increases, can make the orbital shell bistable, with a low-debris and a high-debris equilibrium, and hysteretic. This has two major operational consequences. First, leaving the high-debris equilibrium requires a large cut in launch rates. Second, in the low-debris equilibrium, fragment counts respond with a delay as the launch rate rises past a tipping point. Removing bistability is desirable, and we show that fragment count-indexed admission control can achieve this. The least restrictive such policy lengthens the lag, whereas an exponential tilt of this policy makes the fragment count track its equilibrium with a bounded lag. Furthermore, admitting more launches can reduce the rate of completed missions, and under a unimodality condition a threshold rule on the debris fragment count maximizes this rate at equilibrium.

entries.title: Passivity Control for Synchronous Machine Systems using Battery, Field Current and Governor Actuation
entries.abstract: The passivity of synchronous machines enables power system stability to be established from local conditions. A recent state-feedback design enforces robust passivity using battery actuation at the machine terminal bus. This paper extends that design to a model that includes the field winding and the dynamics of a steam turbine and its governor. The extended model provides two additional actuator signals: the exciter input and the governor input. The nonlinear terms in the model depend on speed and field current deviations, and are represented as bounded uncertainties. Robust positive real conditions are derived in terms of a single algebraic Riccati equation. From its solution, a state-feedback controller is designed in closed form. Numerical results show that, unlike the design with battery actuation alone, the proposed controller leads to passivity at all loading levels when the damping is low.

entries.title: Comparison of Open-Source PSCAD EMT Models for Large-Scale AI Data Centers in Smart Grids
entries.abstract: The rapid deployment of artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) introduces gigawatt-scale, highly nonlinear, and fast-varying electronic loads that challenge grid voltage regulation, frequency stability, and disturbance ride-through. Capturing their transient behavior during grid faults and rapid computational workload swings requires high-fidelity electromagnetic transient (EMT) simulations rather than root mean square models. However, limited methodologies exist to audit the component-level adequacy of EMT AIDC models. This paper proposes a software-agnostic, 41-point fidelity framework spanning 11 categories that synthesizes 37 criteria from an existing modeling guideline with four novel requirements: frequency ride-through compliance, disaggregated fan and chiller cooling loads, temperature-dependent thermal response, and DC information technology (IT) load representations. Applying this framework to the four publicly available AIDC models in PSCAD/EMTDC reveals varying degrees of completeness: while the models capture IT load transitions, uninterruptible power supplies, and transfer switches for bulk stability studies, critical gaps remain in electro-thermal cooling coupling, internal protective relaying, and site-level controls. Addressing these gaps will enable comprehensive protection coordination and ride-through compliance studies.

entries.title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
entries.abstract: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

entries.title: SPICE: Stochastic Policy for Interaction in Cluttered Environments
entries.abstract: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.

entries.title: ADSPICE: A Method of Automatic Differentiation for Gradient-Based Lumped Circuit Optimization with Native SPICE
entries.abstract: This work presents a novel computer-aided design (CAD) tool for gradient-based circuit optimization using SPICE and automatic differentiation, which we term ADSPICE. Automatic differentiation (AD) is a technique for evaluating a derivative by breaking it into its elementary differentiation operations and repeatedly applying the chain rule, in contrast with a finite-difference-based derivative computed from a small perturbation. Native SPICE (realized with ngspice) is equipped with automatic differentiation toward gradient-based optimization, particularly adjoint-mode optimization. This is implemented with custom C code and shared library control, allowing easy integration with existing SPICE infrastructure. We show a computational performance analysis, demonstrating faster optimization vs. an existing finite-difference method, SPICE OPUS, the closest competitor in SPICE optimization tools. The result is a speedup factor of 383x for the largest circuit compared within the state-of-the-art, SPICE OPUS. For circuit sizes above approximately 3,500 nodes, the time taken by ADSPICE optimization decreases with increasing problem size, as a proportion of total computational time. The speed bottleneck is shown to be SPICE solves rather than ADSPICE enhancements. Voltage gradients needed for forward-mode AD are benchmarked against Xyce, another state-of-the-art simulator, using an integrated CMOS operational amplifier test circuit. The results match with a maximum error of 0.203%, further validating the accuracy of our method. ADSPICE is shown to enable SPICE, and SPICE-based simulators, with automatic differentiation for gradient optimization, without requiring creation of a new circuit simulator.

entries.title: Sample-Efficient Model Predictive Control via Proximal Policy Optimization
entries.abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) enables real-time control of complex nonlinear systems but often incurs substantial computational costs due to repeated trajectory simulations. In this paper, we bridge policy optimization in reinforcement learning and sampling-based MPC to improve computational efficiency through sample reuse. Starting from a KL-regularized distributional formulation of trajectory optimization, we derive an exact performance-difference identity based on a signed exponential advantage function. This identity motivates two algorithms, PPO-MPPI and SPO-MPPI, which adapt proximal policy optimization techniques to sampling-based MPC, enabling multiple optimization updates using previously evaluated trajectories without additional forward simulations. We establish population-level monotonic improvement guarantees for both methods and prove convergence to first-order stationarity for PPO-MPPI under fixed-covariance Gaussian sampling distributions. Experiments on quadruped velocity tracking and quadrotor path tracking demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve competitive control performance at substantially lower computational cost than multi-stage sampling approaches. Our results establish a principled connection between policy optimization and sampling-based MPC and highlight the potential of trajectory reuse for sample-efficient predictive control.

entries.title: Reinforcement Learning Optimized Flight Control for Interception of High-Altitude Maneuvering Targets
entries.abstract: We implement and compare two approaches to improving flight control system (FCS) performance using reinforcement meta-learning (meta-RL). Both approaches are evaluated in a terminal phase hypersonic intercept engagement requiring hit-to-kill accuracy against a highly agile maneuvering target. In the first approach (FCS-RL), meta-RL is used to optimize a full FCS that maps acceleration tracking error and other measurements directly to commanded channel deflection rates of change, combining pitch, yaw, and roll control into a single policy. In contrast, the second approach (FCS-3L-RL) starts with a standard FCS (FCS-3L) implementing a three-loop autopilot for pitch and yaw control, but adapts the scheduled autopilot gains in real time using a policy optimized with meta-RL. Both approaches are compared to the FCS-3L in a 6-DOF simulator that captures most factors relevant to guidance and flight control. Simulations show that under ideal conditions the three systems have comparable performance. However, under conditions of aerodynamic uncertainty, radome refraction, or target evasive maneuvers, the FCS-RL significantly outperforms the FCS-3L-RL with improved intercept probability and less control effort. In turn, the FCS-3L-RL outperforms the FCS-3L by a similar margin. Importantly, we demonstrate that both FCS-RL and FCS-3L-RL generalize well to novel engagement scenarios, flight conditions, and target maneuvers that are not experienced during the optimization process.

entries.title: Profile Screening and Frequency-Secure Operating Limit Derivation for Data Center Microgrids
entries.abstract: Rapid power variations from artificial intelligence (AI) workloads pose frequency-security challenges for islanded data-center microgrids. This paper proposes a generator step- response-based framework to rapidly screen candidate load pro- files and derive frequency-secure operating limits for IT workload scheduling. Identified generator responses are superimposed to assess the cumulative frequency effects of successive load changes without repeated dynamic simulations. The framework identifies potentially unsafe intervals and determines allowable load magni- tudes, ramp rates, and minimum event spacing, while accounting for prediction uncertainty and governor limits. Validation on a 2.5 MVA islanded microgrid with eight generator configurations and 14 synthetic AI workload profiles shows that 94.75% of 40,208 assessment windows receive decisive screening labels, with no frequency-violating windows classified as secure.

entries.title: Learning and Control in Physically Coupled Dynamical Systems
entries.abstract: We introduce TAG (Testbed for Autonomous Games), a compact, low-cost robotic platform for studying learning and control in physically coupled dynamical systems. TAG combines an actively tilted and steered ball-in-maze board with a top-mounted rotary inverted pendulum. The pendulum's reaction torque and vibration disturb the board and marble, while the board's tilt, driven by the maze-solving policy, simultaneously disturbs the pendulum's balance. The main challenge in learning control policies for each subsystem is accounting for the impact of one subsystem's dynamics on the other's learning process. To address this challenge, we present complementary reinforcement learning paradigms, leveraging model-based and model-free approaches to learn the control policies for the maze and pendulum, respectively. Our key finding is that introducing the pendulum causes an immediate, sharp drop in the maze policy's success rate, but the policy adapts online and recovers to its pre-coupling performance within a small number of learning episodes. Experimental results show that both policies, trained independently, successfully control the maze board and the pendulum despite their physical coupling.

entries.title: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I/O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification
entries.abstract: Programmable logic controllers (PLCs), the industrial computers that operate power and process plants, often run programs whose source code is no longer available; however, every input and output of the controller is logged continuously. This paper therefore asks whether a large language model (LLM) can recover an executable program in Structured Text (ST), the standard PLC language of IEC 61131-3, from such input/output records (traces) alone and, equally important, how the recovered program can be verified. To answer this question, we build a generate-replay-feedback pipeline. First, the LLM writes a candidate program from a compressed summary of the trace, without ever seeing the original program. The candidate is then executed one control cycle (scan) at a time and compared with the recording, and whenever a mismatch occurs the corresponding part of the trace is returned to the LLM, for at most three revisions. Because every result depends on the software that executes the candidates, we first validate it against two independent open-source PLC runtimes and find no unexplained difference. On this basis, we evaluate 47 third-party programs from two public benchmarks. The recovered programs reproduce the recorded trace exactly in 43 cases and agree with the original on 94% of scans for unseen inputs. The remaining errors, however, lie mostly in program branches that the trace never exercised; once a trace that targets these branches is added, agreement on unseen adversarial inputs rises from 0.80 to 0.98. By contrast, a classical automata-learning baseline without an LLM fits the recording but falls to 0.40 on unseen inputs, which indicates that recovering program structure is the hard part. Finally, on real data from a public water-treatment testbed, the recovered control laws match unseen measurements closely (R² > 0.99) and expose the only actuator attack in the dataset.
entries.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference (TPEC 2027)

entries.title: Adaptive Line Switching for Cascade Mitigation in Power Systems via Graph Reinforcement Learning
entries.abstract: Although cascading failures are relatively rare events in power systems, they pose significant risks and can lead to severe economic and societal consequences within a short period. Therefore, developing effective mitigation strategies to prevent cascade propagation and to minimize their impacts is essential. This paper presents a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based framework for adaptive transmission line switching to mitigate cascading failures. Given the important role of network topology and component interactions in cascading failure propagation in power systems, graph-based DRL approaches, including Graph-DQN, Graph-A2C, and Graph-PPO frameworks, are developed to capture and utilize the topological information of power systems. The proposed frameworks are evaluated on the IEEE 39, 57, and 118 bus systems and benchmarked against the unmitigated case, random and heuristic-based switching strategies as baselines, as well as their corresponding graph-agnostic DRL counterparts. The results demonstrate the importance of incorporating graph information into these mitigation frameworks, leading to reduced cascade size, load loss, and network clustering.

entries.title: Verifiably Safe Decentralized Control via Event-Triggered Topology Switching
entries.abstract: This paper proposes a decentralized event-triggered topology-switching protocol for multi-agent systems under estimation uncertainty. We consider an intermittent communication setting in which each agent switches between connected and disconnected modes and makes communication decisions using locally computable certificates, while the closed-loop state is required to remain safe. The proposed protocol follows a safety-driven triggering principle in which agents reconnect before their certificates reach the safety boundary and disconnect only after recovering to a stricter bound below the safety limit. Our design enables intermittent connectivity while maintaining the estimation error within a certified safety bound and excluding Zeno behavior. We evaluate the proposed protocol on a quadruple-tank example, showing that it keeps all tank deviations within the safety bound while allowing agents to remain disconnected for most of the run.

entries.title: Feedback-Linearised Trajectory Tracking via Model-Informed Robust Geometric DDPC
entries.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DDPC) predicts system responses from recorded trajectories, but nonlinear dynamics can limit the accuracy of fixed linear predictors. This paper studies geometric robust DDPC for trajectory tracking of a fully actuated manipulator using model-based feedback linearisation. A mechanical model maps virtual acceleration commands into joint torques, while recorded data capture residual dynamics arising from imperfect model parameters. The controller minimises worst-case prediction error over an open Grassmannian ball centred at the fitted trajectory subspace. Simulations on a planar 2R manipulator under gravity compare the proposed method with double-integrator model predictive control (MPC) and direct regularised data-enabled predictive control (DeePC). Results show improved tracking over double-integrator MPC despite increased torque effort, while performance relative to DeePC depends on the reference trajectory.
entries.comment: This manuscript has been submitted to the 9th Annual Learning for Dynamics & Control Conference, taking place in Stockholm, Sweden, in June 2027

entries.title: Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling
entries.abstract: The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model, provided that the model has been trained on demonstrations of the agents cooperating. Yet, demonstrations of cooperation are costly and may not exist for tasks that the team has never performed. The conditions under which the agents can combine their capabilities, however, are physical properties of the team and are known before any demonstration is collected. We encode the conditions as constraints on the team trajectories, and we enforce the constraints while sampling from generative models trained on demonstrations of each agent alone. We prove that the proposed method can generate every team trajectory that satisfies the constraints, although the demonstrations contain no cooperation. Hence the constraints determine which team trajectories can be generated, and the demonstrations determine how likely each team trajectory is. Numerical results on two cooperative tasks show the effectiveness of the method, which generates cooperative team trajectories that satisfy the constraints and requires no retraining when agents join or leave the team. Finally, we implement the method on a multi-robot testbed.

entries.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
entries.abstract: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.

entries.title: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation
entries.abstract: Magnetic levitation with six-degrees-of-freedom enables frictionless transport and micrometer-scale positioning in principle, but low-level control is inherently challenging due to its complex and unstable dynamics. Industrial systems typically rely on deep hardware-software co-design, where mover and stator geometries are jointly designed to enable a compact, hand-crafted approximation of the electromagnetic force computation, thereby keeping control computationally tractable at kilohertz rates. However, this approach imposes overly conservative constraints on the operating workspace and the range of supported mover topologies. Instead of reducing the underlying physics to a hand-crafted approximation, we compute the physics directly. We introduce Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator for 6D magnetic levitation. It is used to train the first neural controller for an industrial-grade 6D magnetic levitation system that is learned purely from simulated physics. We show that the learned neural controller transfers zero-shot from simulation to real hardware while satisfying hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz. The learned controller achieves qualitatively new behaviors and even levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists. These results demonstrate that co-design is not a physical necessity for 6D magnetic levitation control. More broadly, control learning from simulated physics can find solutions beyond the reach of control engineering in demanding industrial domains. Source code and demonstration videos are publicly available at https://sites.google.com/view/magflow.
entries.comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/magflow

entries.title: Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Robust Synthesis of Signal Temporal Logic Specifications
entries.abstract: Signal Temporal Logic is a popular framework for describing a robotic system's goals. Once described using a temporal logic framework, synthesis turns the goals into actual steps for the robots to follow. Currently, the state of the art for sound and complete synthesis is using Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), which struggles on long time horizons and large environments, preventing the construction of guaranteed safe plans for long deployments. This paper introduces a new synthesis method using Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) which scales better for long deployments and adapts to environmental changes more quickly. We do this by introducing an encoding method for STL into SMT constraints, and an encoding method for discrete-time dynamical systems modeled as a transition system. We then conduct an empirical comparison of our SMT based methods against the state of the art MILP based methods. Results show that for this class of problems, SMT is an effective encoding strategy that performs the best on long time horizon tasks.

entries.title: On the recursive feasibility and stability of MPC without terminal constraints
entries.abstract: In this paper, we analyze stability and recursive feasibility of a model predictive control (MPC) scheme that does not rely on terminal ingredients – such as terminal constraints or a terminal cost based on a terminal controller. In the proposed formulation, we augment the cost function by a weighted finite tail which is optimized online, and we show it plays the role of a stabilizing terminal cost. Under a relaxed, local dynamic programming condition on the tail, we certify a family of regions – parameterized by the tail's weight coefficient – on which the problem is recursively feasible and the origin is asymptotically stable. These regions are larger as the weight increases: in particular, we show that any state that can be steered within the control horizon to a predefined neighborhood of the origin is contained in a certified region for a sufficiently large weight. Finally, we characterize the closed-loop performance over the certified region, bounding the suboptimality of the closed loop with respect to the infinite-horizon optimal cost. We conclude the discussion by illustrating these results on a simple numerical example.

entries.title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
entries.abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

entries.title: Sim2CBF: From Forward Simulations to Implicit Control Barrier Function Safety Filtering without Model Derivatives
entries.abstract: Failure avoidance in complex robot-environment interactions is challenging because the underlying dynamics are difficult to model accurately, and available predictive models may not provide reliable derivatives. We present Sim2CBF, a failure-avoidance framework that solves the Control Barrier Function (CBF)-Safety Filter (SF) optimization problem using only forward-model evaluations, thereby avoiding differentiation of the predictive model. Specifically, we approximate the CBF constraint using finite differences and local linear interpolation over sampled control inputs while preserving failure-avoidance guarantees. The underlying CBF is implicit and constructed from backup-policy rollouts, enabling the use of expressive predictive models such as physics-based simulators and learned world models. Compared with purely sampling-based SFs, our formulation requires fewer control samples and yields less conservative behavior than direct nominal-backup blending. We evaluate Sim2CBF in simulation, hardware box-toppling, and vision-based control tasks, demonstrating its applicability to contact-rich and learned dynamics, as well as its adaptability to changes in the predictive model.

entries.title: Technical Report of Mobile Manipulator Robot for Industrial Environments
entries.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' mobile manipulator robot, developed at the Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory, Department of Electrical Engineering, Shahid Beheshti University. Hereafter, this platform is referred to as the @Work Robot. The robot targets industrial tasks, with an emphasis on improving efficiency in repetitive or hazardous work environments. It uses a 4-wheel Mecanum drive for omnidirectional movement and a 5-degree-of-freedom manipulator arm with a 3D-printed gripper for object handling and navigation. The electronics consist of custom PCB boards built around ESP32 microcontrollers, together with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX that handles high-level processing and real-time system control. On the software side, Hector SLAM provides mapping and localization, A* handles path planning, and YOLO performs real-time object detection. These modules draw on fused sensor data to deliver robust navigation and reliable collision avoidance. Overall, the system shows effective hardware-software integration, with consistent performance in autonomous navigation, object handling, and task execution in industrial-like settings.
entries.comment: 25 pages, 22 figures, 4 tables. Technical report of Team Auriga's 2025 mobile manipulator (@Work) platform (Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory, Shahid Beheshti University)

entries.title: Capacity Credit of Data-Centre Flexibility: The Role of Workload Scheduling and Usable Battery Energy
entries.abstract: Data centres that offer the same reduction in grid demand can make different contributions to supply adequacy. We estimate the effective load-carrying capability of workload scheduling and on-site batteries by matching expected unserved energy across paired simulations. Longer task deadlines increase capacity credit by giving operators more choice over when to defer and recover work. A fixed evening commitment shifts more work than deadline-based scheduling but delivers a smaller reduction in expected unserved energy. Protected backup reserves leave uninterruptible power supplies with limited capacity credit, while longer discharge durations raise the credit of dedicated batteries at the same response rating. These findings suggest assessing recovery deadlines and dispatchable energy alongside offered demand reductions.

entries.title: Classical heat exchanger fouling-resistance laws as first-moment identities of additive stochastic deposition
entries.abstract: Heat-exchanger fouling is monitored through the fouling resistance, whose record is routinely fitted with the classical linear (Ebert–Panchal) or asymptotic (Kern–Seaton) law, and the shape of the fit is often taken as evidence of the underlying deposition or removal mechanism. We show that it cannot be. If the deposit grows by non-negative, statistically stationary increments, the mean fouling resistance is exactly linear without removal and exactly the Kern–Seaton asymptote under first-order removal, whatever the microscopic deposition law. Shear-driven erosion, per-element detachment, intermittent sloughing and saturation of the surface all give the same mean curve, so a fit identifies a net deposition rate and a relaxation time, and nothing else. Modelling the deposit as a Levy subordinator, we show where the missing information lies and what it costs to retrieve it from monitoring data. Removal mechanisms separate in the variance: sloughing leaves a plateau scatter that persists even for smooth deposition and can be read from a record that saturates. Deposition laws separate only in higher cumulants, which the measurement noise of a thermally reconstructed resistance attenuates; the record needed to distinguish them grows as the fourth power of the conductance error, which places it beyond reach at realistic measurement accuracy. For the time to reach a cleaning limit, the deposition law matters only near the threshold; farther away, the mean rate and its uncertainty dominate the prediction.

entries.title: Transmission Expansion and Energy Storage Planning under Great Britain's Uncertain Energy Transition Pathways
entries.abstract: Long term power system planning must account for uncertainty in electricity demand and generation, while recognising the different investment and commissioning characteristics of transmission and energy storage. This paper develops a multi year stochastic framework for coordinated transmission expansion and energy storage planning and applies it to the Great Britain electricity system to assess investment needs through to 2050. The framework integrates multiple energy transition pathways with an enhanced representation of the GB transmission network and captures the different characteristics of transmission and storage investment over time. The coordinated treatment of transmission and storage is considered as a system level benchmark rather than a centralised investment mechanism. In GB, transmission investment is subject to regulated forward looking planning, while storage is largely developed by market participants in response to market signals. The framework therefore quantifies the potential value of improved coordination and identifies where existing investment signals may not encourage complementary storage deployment. Results across alternative transmission only, storage only and coordinated investment strategies show substantial benefits from joint planning. Compared with transmission only planning, coordinated investment reduces additional transmission capacity by 2%, cumulative expected load shedding by 97%, and total expected system cost by 36%, primarily through avoided unserved energy. Transmission preparation periods affect the timing, but not the final portfolio, of investments. Finally, the energy transition pathway materially influences investment requirements, with Electrification and Efficiency requiring 7% more transmission capacity and 45% more storage energy capacity than Falling Behind.

entries.title: A Discrete Digital Isolator with Shielded Planar Transformer for Gate Driver Applications
entries.abstract: Galvanically isolated gate drivers are required in many power electronics applications. This paper describes an implementation of a digital isolator using discrete components with a planar coreless PCB signal transformer providing the isolation. The use of an electrostatic shield between the transformer windings is shown to provide sufficient common-mode transient immunity to support IGBT half-bridge drivers, an application subject to a severe dV/dt transient during switching. The design is verified through the experimental implementation of a prototype half bridge using two of the proposed discrete digital isolators with SiC power transistors and demonstrates common-mode transient immunity greater than 15 kV/us with very low implementation complexity.

entries.title: Manufacturing Differential Sparsity: Planner-Hardware Co-Design for Efficient World Model Planning
entries.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.

entries.title: MARS: Feature-guided physics-informed deep learning for real-time battery health and lifetime prediction
entries.abstract: Accurate and robust estimation of battery state-of-health (SOH) and remaining useful life (RUL) is essential for safe and cost-effective operation of electrified transportation systems, yet it remains challenging under operating variability, non-stationary aging, and non-Gaussian measurement disturbances. This paper proposes Multi-scale Adaptive Robust State Estimation (MARS), a multi-scale adaptive robust state-estimation framework that couples a dual-branch temporal encoder with an equivalent-circuit-model-constrained differentiable generalized-correntropy adaptive Kalman filter. The encoder disentangles fast intra-cycle voltage-current-temperature dynamics from slow inter-cycle degradation, and the fused degradation context adaptively parameterizes the cycle-level process covariance, measurement covariance, and correntropy bandwidth. Through the unrolled robust filtering recursion, MARS performs physics-consistent state propagation and generalized-correntropy-based innovation correction, while uncertainty decomposition and Monte Carlo dropout provide calibrated prediction intervals for SOH estimation and conditional RUL prediction. Experiments on the NASA and CALCE benchmarks demonstrate improved SOH accuracy, achieving mean absolute error/root mean square error values of 0.72%/0.92% and 0.63%/0.80%, respectively, together with competitive conditional RUL performance against representative data-driven and hybrid baselines. The resulting conditional-RUL prediction intervals achieve coverage probabilities of 100.00% and 99.24% on NASA and CALCE, respectively. Ablation, disturbance-sensitivity, near-end-of-life, and runtime analyses further verify the contribution of each module and the practical inference cost for online battery management.
entries.comment: 14 pages, 10 figures. Published in IEEE Transactions on Transportation Electrification, 2026

entries.title: COAST: Safe Flight Corridor Planner for Fast and Robust Snap Minimized Trajectories
entries.abstract: Current B-Spline trajectory planners face a critical trade-off: they either sacrifice computational speed to maintain strict Safe Flight Corridor (SFC) guarantees, or they abandon hard safety bounds in favor of soft-constraint penalties to achieve real-time performance. We present COAST (Corridor-Optimized Aerially-Safe Trajectories), a B-Spline based, online trajectory planner capable of formulating snap minimized trajectories with SFC guarantees. COAST divides the problem into two stages: an A* based front-end that generates geometrically simple SFCs (represented as a chain of rectangular prisms), and a quadratic programming back-end for control point optimization. To handle the non-convexity of SFC intersections, we leverage the finite support property of B-Splines, to ensure the spline never exits SFC boundaries. The control point optimization incorporates MINVO transforms for kinodynamic bounding, allowing COAST to design non-conservative, dynamically feasible trajectories, while a snap minimization matrix calculation provides flight smoothness. This formulation provides a formal geometric containment guarantee, while ensuring mean trajectory computation times under 5 ms for real-time deployment. We validate our results through high-fidelity simulation experiments. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/byu-magicc/Minimum-Snap-Trajectories
entries.comment: 14 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC 2027)

entries.title: Model Augmentation for thermo-mechanical hysteretic dynamics
entries.abstract: Accurate prediction of thermo-mechanical wafer deformation is essential for sub-nanometer overlay in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. Localized heating expands the wafer, while friction between the wafer and its supporting elastic pillars causes hysteresis. Modeling this is challenging because of the system's large scale, the computational cost of friction-induced hysteresis and the sparse deformation measurements. This work augments a linear thermo-mechanical baseline model with a learning-based structure in a linear fractional representation (LFR) framework, identified from sparse measurements. Simulation results show that the augmented model captures the unmodeled dynamics with hysteretic effects and predicts the deformation significantly more accurately than the baseline.

entries.title: Explicit Dual Model Predictive Path Integral Control
entries.abstract: In this work, we present a fully sampling-based explicit dual control algorithm that combines a particle filter and model predictive path integral control for partially observed nonlinear systems. The key idea is to roll out multiple sampled input sequences from all particles of the particle filter to obtain a belief-averaged control cost that induces caution. The same rollouts are used to sample imagined future measurements, which are drawn from the predictive distribution of the particle belief. This results in a Monte Carlo information term that gives a sample estimate of the expected information gain of each sampled input sequence and thereby induces probing. In contrast to existing explicit dual control schemes, the proposed scheme neither relies on gradients of the dynamics or measurement models nor requires a Gaussian belief. Furthermore, all computations can be parallelized across input sequences, particles, and imagined measurements, which makes the scheme amenable to real-time implementation on suitable hardware. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in a simulation example of a planar terrain-aided navigation task.

entries.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
entries.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted–real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves 2.67× and 1.27× query speedups over the respective synchronous π_(0.5) and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with 1.52×–1.93× query speedup.

entries.title: Data-driven model reduction: An identification perspective using Generalized Bases of Orthonormal Functions
entries.abstract: This paper proposes a data-driven model order reduction approach based on system identification concepts. A revised equation error formulation is introduced, in which the model is parameterized using Generalized Bases of Orthonormal Transfer Functions (GBOFs). The generalized reduction problem is formulated in the Hambo frequency domain associated with the GBOF transform. The frequency-domain fit of the reduced-order model is adjusted through the selection of the basis poles. A fit indicator depending on these poles is introduced, providing valuable heuristic guidance for their selection.

entries.title: Connections Between Instrumental Variable, Pseudo-Linear Regression, and Prediction Error Methods in Terms of Their Minimized Criteria
entries.abstract: This paper explores the connections between the criteria directly or indirectly minimized by Prediction Error (PE), Instrumental Variable (IV), and Pseudo-Linear Regression (PLR) algorithms for the identification of output-error models. By definition, PE methods aim to minimize the variance of the prediction error. In contrast, the correlation functions appearing in the stationarity conditions of IV and PLR algorithms are not the gradients of any underlying loss function involving a signal variance. Nevertheless, if the true system lies in the model set, we show that one IV algorithm minimizes asymptotically the variance of an unmeasurable signal called the equivalent prediction error. This signal was introduced previously to analyze the bias distribution of PLR schemes. It turns out that, regardless of whether the true system lies in the model set, some iterative IV and PLR algorithms aim to minimize the prediction error variance and can therefore be interpreted as indirect PE algorithms.

entries.title: Learning Regions of Attraction for Transverse Feedback Linearization under Controller Singularities
entries.abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl
entries.comment: 27 pages (10 main + references + appendix), 1 figure, 8 tables

entries.title: Optimal Energy and LLM Task Scheduling for Multiple Cloud Data Centers
entries.abstract: This paper studies coordinated Large Language Model (LLM) training-task scheduling and facility operation for geographically distributed cloud data centers (CDCs). The central question is how two scheduling flexibilities - cross-CDC task transfer and task reordering - affect service and economic outcomes when remote execution remains subject to compute, bandwidth, energy, and zone-temperature constraints. We formulate a mixed-integer optimization model that jointly determines task outcomes, heterogeneous-node assignment, execution timing, pre-execution data transfer, node activation, and facility operation. A deterministic 24-hour case study contains 3 CDCs, 15 heterogeneous graphics processing unit (GPU) nodes, 4 thermal zones per CDC, and 103 tasks. In this instance, enabling transfer increases net profit by 57.9% relative to the otherwise matched no-transfer variant and increases completed tasks from 76 to 103. The more restrictive no-transfer FIFO-prefix variant completes 14 tasks and yields negative profit. The proposed schedule transfers 39 tasks, achieves 70.3% node utilization, and maintains zone temperatures within 24°C-27°C. These fixed-instance results indicate that cross-CDC transfer and task-reordering flexibility can improve the modeled profit and task-completion outcomes under the studied conditions.

entries.title: Solver-Free and Cost-Aware Online Scheduling of AI Data Center Tasks
entries.abstract: AI data centers receive computing tasks continuously, whereas solver-based optimization takes time to run and electricity is priced per settlement period. This paper bridges this timing gap through a solver-free online optimization rule inspired by dual decomposition. The rule assigns each task a start period upon arrival to optimize energy cost subject to operational constraints, shifting flexible tasks toward low-price periods while keeping high-priority tasks on schedule. Simulations on the A100 GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks) show that the proposed rule keeps GPU and CPU use within capacity while scheduling tasks at low cost. Compared with a multi-timescale optimization benchmark, it achieves a lower cost and, because it needs no solver, much less computation time.

entries.title: From Temperature-Limited to Battery-Limited Legged Locomotion
entries.abstract: On legged robots, sustained locomotion often ends in thermal shutdown rather than battery depletion: the heat of walking concentrates in a few joint motors, which overheat long before the battery is empty. We train thermally aware locomotion policies by reinforcement learning without ever observing temperature, and demonstrate this on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. We first identify a coupled 13-node lumped RC thermal network, fitted on two runs of a single robot and calibrated against the measured electrical power, that predicts all twelve motor temperatures with a mean RMSE below 1 °C across different robot instances, gaits, payloads, and speeds. Under a sustained gait, the temperatures the motors will settle at follow directly from the gait-averaged squared torques and joint speeds. Our core contribution is a reward that drives down the hottest predicted asymptotes: thermal time constants exceed the credit-assignment horizon of reinforcement learning by orders of magnitude, but predicted asymptotes respond to torque and joint speed within a single gait cycle, so the policy learns to lower and spread heat with no temperature input. On the robot, the policy turns sustained locomotion from temperature-limited to battery-limited: with a 5 kg payload at 1 m/s, a learned baseline reaches thermal shutdown after 19 minutes (1.1 km), whereas our policy runs the battery down after 174 minutes (10.0 km) with its hottest motor 14 °C below the shutdown threshold in a 26 °C room; on an unloaded factory circuit with stairs and ramps, the baseline overheats after 25 laps (6.2 km), while our policy completes 47 (11.2 km) on one battery with 22 °C of margin.
entries.comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Supplementary video in the ancillary files. Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24274994

entries.title: Safely Mitigating Grid Imbalance: A Hybrid Distributional Wide-Margin Recourse Approach
entries.abstract: This paper proposes the Multi-Agent Distributional Wide-Margin Policy Gradient (MADWMPG) framework: a dual-policy hybrid imitation and safe reinforcement learning (IL-SRL) method designed for safely mitigating grid imbalance in multiphase active distribution networks with distributed soft open points (SOPs). The framework comprises a wide-margin constraint barrier recourse (WCBR) module that seeks the maximal separation of constraint-compliant and unsafe actions and learns to proactively suppress exploratory violations. The framework addresses operational volatility using a novel adaptation of noncrossing quantile regression (NQR) distributional critics that track the complete distribution of policy returns. The set of behavior and recourse policies integrates an instantaneous physics-based and differentiable action projection mechanism that generates SOP constraint-compliant actions without relying on active learning. Policy safety is made responsive using an enhancement of conventional experience replay, and the safety performance of the framework is supported by probabilistic bounds derived in the paper. The proposed framework was trained and tested on a modified multiphase IEEE 123-bus test feeder. Results demonstrate its superiority to conventional reinforcement learning and SRL methods and show that it is highly competitive against the nonlinear AC optimal power flow.

entries.title: Grid-Responsive Pricing of Dynamic Wireless Charging with Coupled Residential Demand
entries.abstract: Dynamic wireless charging (DWC) is an emerging technology that enables electric vehicles (EVs) to recharge while traveling. Its unique operational model creates two revenue streams for DWC operators through lane access tolls and electricity sales. However, these prices influence not only traffic flow and roadway energy delivery but also how much EV charging moves to homes instead, potentially within the same distribution network. Neglecting this coupling can underestimate grid loading and compromise pricing decisions. We develop a coupled traffic, EV energy, driver-response, and AC distribution network model with a model predictive control (MPC) framework that jointly optimizes DWC tolls and charging prices while explicitly accounting for displaced residential charging and network losses. Using 78 days of I-210 West traffic data, we show that conventional MPC exceeds feeder loading limits on 52 days, whereas the proposed residential load aware controller eliminates these violations with only 0.6% lower operator revenue. Under a more constrained feeder configuration, it eliminates 50 overloaded days with a 0.9% revenue reduction. Sensitivity analyses highlight the importance of accurate residential demand estimation and feeder loss modeling, while peak-aware pricing further reduces daily peak loading by 3.7% relative to the base load. These results demonstrate the value of coordinated pricing that captures the interaction between roadway and residential charging.
entries.comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Submitted to the IEEE Power & Energy Society General Meeting (PESGM) 2027

entries.title: Benchmarking a Grid Foundation Model for AC Optimal Power Flow: Feasibility and Warm-Start Results on Synthetic Texas and South Carolina Grids
entries.abstract: Learning-based surrogates for alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF) are often judged by the gap between their objective value and that of a nonlinear solver, which does not show that a prediction satisfies power balance and network limits. This paper tests whether predictions from the pretrained foundation model GridSFM-Open 1.1.0, recently released by Microsoft, are feasible AC-OPF operating points and whether they are useful initial values for a nonlinear solver. The model was evaluated zero-shot and after fine-tuning on 10, 100, and 1,000 labeled scenarios (FT10, FT100, and FT1000) on 500 scenarios for each of two synthetic grids, ACTIVSg2000 (Texas) and ACTIVSg500 (South Carolina), with Ipopt, MATPOWER MIPS, and pandapower PIPS as solver references. The lowest Texas median cost gap, 0.44% for FT100, coincided with thermal violations in 24.1% of cases and a median maximum bus power mismatch of 89 MW and 197 Mvar. Texas zero-shot predictions had a median maximum mismatch of 648 MW and 1,641 Mvar, and every South Carolina case violated a thermal limit for every model variant.
